subject: Install treadle M3/M4 and battery the rule-target-blocking gap

Install treadle M3/M4 and battery the rule-target-blocking gap

The next declared semantic freeze in README.md is closure-safe rule-target
blocking, deferred by the accepted challenge profile with
RULE_TARGET_BLOCKING_UNSUPPORTED. This installs the minimal treadle module
set for that work and runs its first two steps. It changes no PFF value,
gate, diagnostic, ordering rule, or public API; src/poietics is untouched.

Assembly (skills/assembly, minimal-install rule): M3 checker plus M4
prompt-cores. The gate is skipped (one actor, one session) and the driver is
skipped (no endpoint, and the generator is the agent). docs/TREADLE_ASSEMBLY_V0.1.md
records the module table and the three glue answers.

Battery (skills/example-battery): thirteen structures given extensionally as
ground programs -- six positives, five near-misses forming five minimal pairs
with pairwise distinct shapes, and two boundaries recorded OPEN. Both walls
of the profile's stated risk corridor are built: N1 is the structure an
unclosed rule blocker wrongly admits, P3 the one that blocking every face of
the rule wrongly excludes. Digests come only from scripts/battery_digest.py.

Denotation tests (skills/denotation-tests): every instance is replayed
through poietics.ground.evaluate. The frozen half of the hand-materialised
lowering is checked against the real compiler -- instance N3 is rebuilt as a
package, validated, compiled, and asserted equal atom for atom and rule for
rule. Boundary instances record observed behaviour under three candidate
sourcings and assert none. A standing probe pins the compiler's existing
deferral so the effect cannot be admitted silently.

subject: Discharge the pin's audits against independent models
body:
Discharge the pin's audits against independent models

Two of the cycle's protocols cannot be discharged by the agent that authored
the work: semantic-round-trip needs a back-translator that has never seen the
intent, and an author reviewing their own pin is worth less than one who has
not. The owner supplied a key and an approved model list, so those roles now
go to external models. Analysis only; src/poietics is untouched.

Roles. deepseek-v4-pro:0813 for the independent minimal-pair review, the
verdict-ledger audit, and the round-trip comparator; glm-5.2 and
kimi-k2.7-code as two isolated back-translators, chosen as different models
rather than two samples of one. The deepseek tag is the dated checkpoint,
per the treadle field report: the undated tag silently moved, which is the
drift the eval criteria prohibit.

Findings acted on. The ledger audit found two real route-typing errors --
V5 and V6 claimed EXHAUSTION for what are single- and two-structure
witnesses -- and both are retyped WITNESS with the correction attributed. It
also confirmed, with the profile in hand, that admitting the pin falsifies
the profile's "face clearance is the only path" sentence, and that the pin
states it at the right strength.

Round trip. Round 1 came back DIVERGENT and earned its keep: the two isolated
readers split on the boundary instances, which exposed a defect in the packet
rather than the clause -- it named the evaluator but never said that an atom
no gate places and no rule defines is unfounded, hence excluded. The packet
now says so, the round-1 copy is frozen because a superseded audit input is
part of the record, and round 2 returned ROUNDTRIP_CLEAN with both readers
matching every recorded verdict. The record states plainly which conclusion
round 2 therefore cannot support: the boundary readings, since the added rule
settles them outright. Round 1's split is the honest evidence there, and it
argues on the merits for resolving OPEN-1 toward a required field.

The independent minimal-pair review returned YES on all six pairs and
proposed one further contrast, B1 against P1. It is recorded as a boundary
contrast and machine-checked rather than adopted as a near-miss, because
giving B1 an intent would decide OPEN-1, which is the owner's to decide. Its
steering check answered "no finding", and the review record says why that is
not independent confirmation against FIND-1: the profile was not among its
inputs, so it could not have run that check.

Provenance. No board: none of these jobs has an exit code, and wrapping five
one-shot calls in a stage table would invert the minimal-install rule. What
the driver's discipline does supply is the ledger, and that is reimplemented
-- zoo/reviews/calls.jsonl hash-chains every call with model tag, parameters,
and prompt and reply hashes. tests/test_review_ledger.py verifies the chain
offline, reproduces the round-2 back-translator prompts byte for byte from
the tree, and proves the isolation guard catches a planted leak. The key
lives only in the process environment and is in no committed file.

No external call is an acceptance command. Acceptance stays battery_digest
--verify, green on 15 rows, and the unittest suite, 296 tests passing.

subject: Install first authority, audit it, and revise the pin to v0.2
body:
Install first authority, audit it, and revise the pin to v0.2

The core specification is now in the tree, byte-exact against the SHA-256 the
accepted profile cites as first authority. tests/test_authority.py pins it and
declares the one cited authority still absent, so authority can no longer
drift silently. Analysis only; src/poietics is untouched and the compiler
still fails closed on every rule-target undercut and wound.

The milestone map was wrong and is corrected. The specification carries an
Implementation sequence, and it is not the README's freeze queue -- the freeze
queue orders the work inside its milestone 4. Milestones 1 to 3 are done, 4 is
partial, and the specification places the discernment report next, before the
empirical pack. docs/CORE_SPEC_AUDIT_V0.1.md carries the map, the sixteen-case
conformance coverage (nine covered, one partial, six not, each blocker named),
and two benign implementation deviations.

Two freezes moved. The defect and problem-face lifecycle is fully specified --
effect, retention rule, and required post-discharge statuses -- so it is
dispatchable and jumps the queue ahead of rule-target blocking, which still
needs a field the specification does not carry. Revocation is partly
unblocked: the effect shape is known and lands on faces, and only the
selection algorithm and token grammar are missing.

Pin v0.2 supersedes v0.1, which stays as history. First authority forces the
bridge -- it requires a closure gate for every default-negative literal and
supplies no rule field to carry one -- which is what moves the record from a
named OPEN item to a pin. It also refutes two of the four sourcings outright.
The pin takes an optional field, so no already-accepted package changes status,
and refuses a blocking challenge against an unblockable rule at admission
rather than compiling one that does nothing.

Independent audits caught three things and all three are applied. The
spec-conformance audit found two of five authority claims OVERSTATED: the
optionality and the admission rule are analogies, not readings, and both are
now tagged as normative choices with OPEN-1 reopened as narrowed rather than
resolved. The ledger audit retyped V4 to WITNESS and corrected V13, where
HAND_PENDING_MECHANIZATION had been used as a route when it is a checker for
PROOF. The same reviewer had passed that row in v0.1; single-reviewer audits
are not exhaustive and are not recorded as if they were.

Round 3 of the round-trip returned DIVERGENT and its finding is refuted: the
comparator claimed a failed closure excludes readiness, when the specification
calls that table deliberately asymmetric and sends readiness to the protected
open set. The twin settles it, kimi-k2.7-code was right, glm-5.2 and the
comparator were not. The round is recorded DIVERGENT rather than upgraded --
overriding an audit on the author's say-so would defeat it -- with the plain
statement that no divergence was found against the clause. ClosureAsymmetryTests
pins the gate three of the four readings got wrong.

Battery: seventeen instances, seven pairs, one refused at admission. B1 and B2
stopped being boundaries once first authority settled what an absent record
means; the one remaining boundary asks what the record is a closure of.

subject: Build the discernment report
body:
Build the discernment report

The specification's next milestone, and the one thing in the queue blocked on
nothing: no missing field, no freeze, no owner decision. "The evaluator SHALL
not return only a status label" -- poietics.explain is what it returns
instead. New module; the engine's semantics are untouched and a test holds
that nothing in pff or ground imports it.

The report carries the conflict axis, live cases with their exact premises,
certificate, faces, frame, grade and source rule, blocked cases classified by
every applicable blocker rather than the first, open dependencies,
certificates, closures and challenges, wounds, orphans, counter cases, and
the shared provenance DAG. Cycles collapse into one SCC summary node, so a
cyclic program still yields a finite report.

Conformance case 6 moves from partial to covered: a live atom with a live
explicit contrary now reads CONFLICTED, and the no-explosion half is asserted
by comparing the compiled rule set with and without the contrary. Ten covered,
zero partial, six not -- and the six are blocked on structures the engine
cannot yet represent, not on the report, which is why milestone 5 is recorded
partial rather than done.

Four blocker codes cannot be emitted by this build. They are defined because
the specification defines them and listed in UNREACHABLE_BLOCKERS with a
reason each, so a reader is never left thinking their conditions were checked
and found absent. A test asserts none of them is emitted anywhere.

Three report fields are readings the specification names without defining --
counter_cases, orphans, and the protects_open edge -- and each is marked at
the point it is built. revocations can never be populated while revoke is
deferred, and says so.

The independent conformance review returned CONFORMS on all six audit items
and no truth-inference, and caught one thing: the unfounded fallback asserted
that an excluded case with no other blocker "can only happen through such a
cycle", stated as if the specification settled it. It does not, and the claim
was also wrong -- that state is unreachable, because no finding means the case
rule is definitely enabled and an enabled rule with an excluded head is a
derived-status collision the evaluator refuses first. The branch now says
exactly that and raises. To make the unreachability argument safe rather than
hopeful, each case body read from the package is cross-checked against the
compiled rule case, and drift raises.

subject: Battery and pin the defect lifecycle
body:
Battery and pin the defect lifecycle

The freeze the core specification already settles. It needs no new package
field, no registry change, and no amendment to an accepted sentence, which is
what separates it from rule-target blocking; and it is conformance case 12.
Analysis only: src/poietics is untouched and the compiler still fails closed
on every defect.

Battery: twelve structures, four pairs, two boundaries. Instance N1 is
conformance case 12 verbatim -- problem record LIVE, discharge LIVE, open
status EXCLUDED. The diagnosis survives while the obligation closes.

The battery needed a second refutation mode. A reading can fail by collapsing
a pair the pin separates, or by splitting one the pin keeps together.
Retention is an invariance -- "a later discharge does not delete the
diagnosis" -- so the reading that derives the effect from open-challenge is
refuted by inventing a difference where none may exist, not by missing one.
A battery that only knew collapse could not test an invariance at all. The
independent reviewer was asked directly whether that mode is a legitimate
refutation or a dodge, and judged it legitimate, with reasons.

Pin: one generated atom, two generated rules, and the validation error profile
§4.2 already declared due. The specification's `discharge_domain(w)` and
`face_discharged(w)` name no record, so binding them to the challenge's own
discharge closure and to the compiled discharged(c) are declared normative
choices, not readings.

The conformance audit found two things. It called the claim that a defect
blocks nothing OVERSTATED, and it was right: the effect table simply contains
no blocker, and an omission is not a statement. That claim is now tagged as a
clarification, with its two supporting arguments and both of their weaknesses
stated, and the corridor table says the same. It called the no-registry-change
claim UNSUPPORTED, which was a scoping artifact -- it held the specification
and the pin, not the registry -- so the claim is now checked in the repository
instead of asserted.

It also read the pin as incomplete because its bindings are open. The status
line drops the complete/incomplete binary rather than argue it, and the
disagreement is recorded rather than quietly resolved: term-pinning ties
incompleteness to an unjustified source-level bridge, and this record needs no
bridge, but the reviewer read "open item" more broadly. Both readings are on
the page; the owner decides which matters.

The minimal-pair review returned YES on all four pairs and proposed one new
pair, built as boundary B2. It earns its place: with every obligation
discharged the two candidate indexings agree, so the open question of B1 bites
only on a partial discharge. That narrows what acceptance has to decide.

subject: Build the first object-level predicate pack
body:
Build the first object-level predicate pack

Milestone 6. Eleven registered predicates, the four pack rules, and the
reference fixture whose required result is that an adverse outcome
manufactures no blame or refutation. It reproduced that table exactly on the
first run: package failure LIVE, component failure SUSPENDED, defect
SUSPENDED, refutation SUSPENDED.

A pack adds no engine behaviour, and a test holds that -- registry data,
package data, and a fixture builder, with no evaluator change and no new
compiler role. Nothing in pff, ground, or explain imports it.

Conformance cases 13 and 14 are now covered, taking the suite to twelve of
sixteen. Case 13 has both its arms: an open localisation certificate suspends
the component failure, an exact failed one excludes it, and the package
failure survives either way. Case 14 shows a live defect and a live rival do
not make a refutation, and that dropping any single premise of the
five-premise conjunction blocks it -- while all five together do produce it,
so the rule is not vacuously unsatisfiable.

The specialised gaps are exercised end to end for the first time. A
localisation_gap blocks only the component case and a recovery_gap only the
refutation case, with the package failure untouched by either or both.
Raising one changes the face blocker closure's exact materialised set, and
the closure recomputes to fail if the fixture pretends otherwise; that is the
checker working, so the fixture updates its members rather than routing
around it.

The tests query the discernment report as well as the status, because
milestone 5's exit condition is that every conformance fixture explains its
distinction and these are the fixtures. The report names the missing
localisation as an open dependency, and charges a raised gap to the face.

Three readings are marked where the specification leaves a choice: "derived"
is not one of the four computability classes, so those predicates are FIN with
primitive_allowed false; two of the four argument prefixes are pack naming
conventions since only account: and outcome: are fixed by the specification's
example; and one sort spans component, explanation, and package because the
specification's own text does. The independent review judged all three sound
and found no choice presented as settled.

It also found one thing missing, and it was right: the pack shipped the
fixture without the result table the specification ships beside it. A
conformance fixture without its required result is half a fixture -- a
consumer gets the package and not what it should produce. The table is now
module data, and a test transcribes the specification independently to check
the shipped table is the specified one rather than whatever the engine emits.

Also fixes both dependency-boundary guards, which matched the module name as a
substring and so tripped on the word appearing in prose. They now parse
imports, and one of them proves it catches a planted import.

Acceptance: both batteries verified; 423 tests pass.

subject: Milestone 7: canonical package bytes, hash, and the append-only replay fold
body:
Milestone 7: canonical package bytes, hash, and the append-only replay fold

Closes the specification's seventh milestone and its sixteenth conformance
case. Thirteen of sixteen cases are now covered; the three that remain are
blocked on record-model gaps, not on engineering.

poietics.canonical
  One canonical document per package: UTF-8, sorted keys, no insignificant
  whitespace, collections sorted by stable ID, set-valued reference arrays
  sorted by exact reference, and ordered predicate arguments left in
  signature order. Floats are refused in semantic positions and permitted in
  metadata, which is non-semantic. The package hash is sha256 over the
  semantic form, which omits metadata and parent_package_hash. The
  evaluation certificate binds a query and its status to that hash and to
  one registry, and carries no score, confidence, or acceptance.

poietics.replay
  Folds a contiguous append-only log up to a cut into one candidate Package
  through add, revoke, set_cut, and checker_result, and refuses a log it
  cannot fold with one of nine typed codes. Equal prefixes fold to equal
  canonical packages and equal evaluations. A folded package is handed to
  validate_package like any other and receives no privilege for having been
  folded. Six choices the specification leaves open are marked in the module
  rather than made quietly.

The round-trip is asserted on the semantic bytes. Metadata is non-semantic,
is excluded from the hash, and is carried by no event operation, so a fold
neither can nor need reproduce it; a test records the exclusion as a fact
rather than an omission.

Dependency direction is one-way and guarded: no engine module imports
canonical or replay, so no status can depend on how a package is serialised,
and the guard also forbids reaching canonical transitively through replay.

Independent review (deepseek-v4-pro:0813, temperature 0, seed 17) returned
five CONFORMS and two DEVIATES. Both DEVIATES are refuted in writing in
zoo/reviews/CANONICAL_REPLAY_REVIEW_RESPONSE.md:

  - a closure record has no payload_hash field in the specification's own
    package model, so the fold cannot bind one without growing the model;
    the closure's payload is carried inline by selector and members. Filed
    as audit deviation AU-3, a specification question for the owner.
  - the base partition is package data with its own section and placement
    rule, not the evaluator's readout; the fold stores no derived status.

One narrative finding is accepted and acted on: a log names neither its
package nor its registry, so the equal-prefix property is relative to the
fold's parameters. The scope is now stated in the module and asserted by
FoldParameterTests, which shows the parameters are load-bearing rather than
leaving the scope implicit.

489 tests, 2004 subtests pass. Both batteries verify.

subject: Milestone 8: hold the independence condition, escalate the deliverable
body:
Milestone 8: hold the independence condition, escalate the deliverable

The work began as "build the problem extension pack, the last milestone". It
ends with the condition mechanically enforced, the deliverable put to the
owner as a specification conflict, two implementation defects fixed, and two
package-model questions filed.

Milestone 8's exit condition, enforced
  tests/test_pack_independence.py holds "added independently without changing
  the core evaluator": no engine module imports a pack, contains a pack
  predicate, argument prefix, checker id, or registry id, and the installed
  pack exposes no callable that decides a status. Each guard states its own
  limit in its docstring; a guard whose limits are unstated is read as
  covering what it does not. The token matcher matches prefixes with their
  opening quote, after three false positives from Python annotations.

The deliverable, escalated rather than decided
  The problem pack is the only extension row the specification says enough
  about to build, and its rules are placed by other sections inside the core
  compiler: the defect effect is in Deterministic compilation, the retention
  rule names no certificate that RuleRecord requires, the defect discharge row
  is already in the initial core registry, and structural problem ordering has
  no normative content anywhere in the document. Building it would mean
  editing compile.py under this milestone's independence banner - the failure
  the milestone exists to prevent. But the Extension packs table lists problem
  as a pack and makes it a milestone deliverable, so this is a conflict
  between two specification statements and the owner's to resolve.
  docs/MILESTONE_8_FINDINGS_V0.1.md states it with the counter-case attached.

Fixed: two specified blocker codes were never emitted
  localisation_missing and recovery_missing were declared unreachable because
  "no pack is installed" - a reason that was false, and that was never the
  relevant condition. The condition is face kind, which is core v0.1
  vocabulary; the report already computed wounded_transport that way and the
  registry's required_face_kind contract already forces the pairing. The
  engine was inconsistent with itself, not short of information.
  _wounded_transport_faces becomes _refined_face_blockers, table-driven, and
  both codes are emitted alongside face_blocked rather than instead of it.

Filed for the owner
  AU-4: validate_package refuses the specification's own closed-negative
  literal example with unresolved_reference, because a __pff__: atom is not a
  package record. Verified by construction with a positive control. This
  narrows two queued freezes to the compiler-generated route rather than
  blocking them.

  AU-5: registry_id is the only registry contribution to the canonical bytes,
  and the registry reaches compilation at two points. One package, one
  registry_id, one package hash, two registries differing only in whether
  undercut admits repair - and clear(face:target@5) comes out LIVE under one
  and EXCLUDED under the other. Conformance case 16 is unaffected and stays
  covered; what narrows is the evaluation certificate's determinism claim.

  Defect pin OPEN-6: conformance case 12 cannot decide the discharge_domain
  binding it appears to test. Replayed through the real evaluator, every gate
  value gives EXCLUDED once discharged; only an undischarged query separates
  them, and case 12 does not contain one. A wrong binding would pass.

Independent review (deepseek-v4-pro:0813) returned two CONFORMS and four
MISSING, and changed the findings document: it was right that the report had
closed a question it should have escalated, and right that two implementation
facts were reading as specification readings. Both corrected. Its reasoning
about case 16 is refuted in writing - checker results are byte-identical in
both runs - while the warning underneath it is accepted. Disposition at
zoo/reviews/MILESTONE_8_REVIEW_RESPONSE.md.

508 tests, 2654 subtests pass. Both batteries verify.

subject: Build cli.py: the five specified commands, closing the completion criterion
body:
Build cli.py: the five specified commands, closing the completion criterion

The specification's completion criterion asks that "one clean checkout can RUN
the core conformance fixtures, emit canonical package hashes, produce
deterministic LIVE, EXCLUDED, and SUSPENDED results, distinguish explicit
conflict from blocking, and explain package failure without inventing component
blame or refutation". Every clause but the first was already met; nothing could
be run without pytest and a PYTHONPATH. This is the interface the criterion
means, and the module table names it.

poietics.cli
  validate, evaluate, why, canonicalise, replay. The composition root: the one
  place the engine and an installed pack are wired together, and the only
  module that may import both. It decides nothing - every command is a thin
  path through parse, validate, compile, evaluate, explain.

  stdout is always the artifact and stderr always the commentary, so every
  command pipes. Exit codes: 0 success, 1 the package was refused with its
  typed issues, 2 usage, 3 unreadable input. A failed checker is not a refusal
  - it is semantic data, and exits 0 with the status it produces.

  why emits the fourteen fields the discernment report section lists, in its
  order. evaluate reports source atoms and compiler-generated gate atoms
  separately, partitioned on the reserved __pff__: prefix, so a reader is not
  filtering scaffolding out by hand.

Reading a package back
  Every command needs a package from disk, and the canonical form had no
  reader. canonical.py gains record_from_document, package_from_document, and
  parse_package - the serial form now goes both ways. replay.py's private
  parser delegates to the shared one rather than keeping a second copy of the
  record-field mapping, which removes the divergence risk; the fold keeps its
  own obligations on top (a derived status may never appear as an event, and
  every refusal carries its sequence number).

The layer map is now single-sourced
  cli.py imports a pack, which the independence guards correctly refused. The
  exemption is principled - a composition root is where wiring belongs - and
  is safe only because nothing imports it back, which is now asserted, along
  with __main__ holding one import and no logic. Five boundary suites had been
  keeping five private copies of the layer list; they all now read
  ABOVE_THE_ENGINE from tests/test_pack_independence.py, and a stale exemption
  left by a rename fails.

Independent review (deepseek-v4-pro:0813) returned six CONFORMS and found a
real conformance break: --registry-id was required, so the specification's own
invocation `pff replay EVENTS --cut N --output PACKAGE` failed. No event names
a registry, so the fold must take one - but "the caller must supply it" is not

AU-5: work the registry-pinning question up for decision

Taking the approved ordering, AU-5 first. Nothing here is implemented and no
semantics is frozen: the deliverable is a decision made decidable, which is a
candidate pin with its options, plus the measurements behind them.

The finding is narrower than the audit claimed
  The audit said two registry fields reach compilation and can move a status
  under a fixed registry_id. Only one can. Both arms of the branch that reads
  known_challenge_kinds end the compile before a program exists, so that read
  chooses a failure mode rather than a status, and its AssertionError arm is
  unreachable because validation refuses an unknown challenge kind first.

  Established by instrumenting PredicateRegistry.__getattribute__ and flipping
  the phase the instant validate_package returns: a package with no discharge
  touches NO registry attribute after admission; one with a discharge touches
  only the discharge-compatibility cluster. An attribute never read after
  admission cannot move an admitted package's status.

  A four-route adversarial sweep failed to refute it, each route running code
  rather than reading it. Two negative results worth keeping: computability_class
  and rule_schema_ids are inert, read by no module in pff/, ground/ or explain/;
  and swapping an alien registry in after validation, with every predicate field
  mutated, compiles to an object-equal GroundProgram.

  So the blast radius is one table - the discharge compatibility table, which is
  the one structure the specification says "may grow only through a registry
  version change". The specification's own safeguard is aimed at exactly the
  right place and lands where nothing observes it.

What makes it decidable
  This codebase already pins a registry version, in binding/plan.py, and stamps
  it into every EvidenceTask that goes out to a checker. Nothing carries it
  forward - not finalize, not the Package, not the canonical bytes, not the
  certificate. The version is worth pinning when a question is asked and not
  worth pinning when the answer is certified.

Independent review (deepseek-v4-pro:0813) returned the most useful round of the
series, and the pin says materially less than it did:

  - It caught a self-contradiction. The pin claimed to attach no recommendation
    and then wrote that an option "should probably be rejected". Having just
    been corrected for closing a question I should have escalated, I
    over-corrected into pretending to have no view while expressing one. The
    view is now stated openly, as a view, separate from the options.
  - It found two facts the pin had missed. registry_id already ends in a
    version-like suffix (0.1) that does not agree with registry.version (1),
    and nothing checks them - so this build already carries two disagreeing
    version notions, and I wrote a pin about adding a third without noticing.
    And the certificate's registry_id is redundant with its package_hash, which
    makes the gap's description more exact rather than larger.
  - It proposed a fifth option, enforcing the existing suffix, which is the
    cheapest of the five and needs no new field anywhere.
  - It supplied the strongest argument against the pin's own premise: an
    operational precondition and an evidential contract answer different
    questions, so both layers can be right. Recorded rather than rebutted; the
    asymmetry now raises the question instead of settling it.
  - It caught an inference stated as a reading - that a consumer cannot fetch
    and verify a code registry, which the specification nowhere says. Dropped.

OPEN-1: measure the rule-target choice, then reverse the recommendation on it

Next in the approved order. Nothing implemented, nothing frozen: v0.3 is a
candidate pin that supersedes v0.2 and now recommends the opposite option.

What v0.2 left unmeasured
  Its central argument for an optional RuleRecord.blocker_closure was that
  admitting the term "changes the status of no already-accepted package". True,
  and never measured. tests/test_rule_target_blast_radius.py measures both
  options across every package fixture the repo can build with no arguments -
  22 of them, a lower bound since builders needing arguments are skipped:

    optional: 0 rules gain a conjunct, 0 packages invalidated
    required: 40 rules need a closure they lack, all 22 packages invalidated,
              40 new ClosureRecords to author

AU-4 narrows rather than blocks
  The pin's clear-rule(r) negates a compiler-generated atom, which AU-4 says a
  package cannot do. It does not block the pin: clear-face already emits
  exactly that shape from the compiler, with no validation in the path. What
  AU-4 removes is the alternative - a package-authored version of this pin is
  inexpressible, so the compiler-generated route is the only one available.

Independent review changed the recommendation
  This is the first review in the series to do so. It refuted the pin's own
  central argument, and I checked the refutation against the specification
  rather than accepting it:

  - The FaceRecord precedent argument was INVALID. It ran "faces are required
    to name a closure because faces are selective; rules are not selective;
    therefore optional". The reviewer: that conflates existence selectivity
    with targetability. The specification says "For every face f, the compiler
    creates has-open-challenge(f) and clear(f)" - no exception, no opt-in.
    There is no unblockable face, so the precedent is about targetability and
    cuts toward required. An optional field creates something the face system
    has no analogue for: an unblockable rule. Argument withdrawn, refutation
    pinned by a test.

  - The measured cost is a migration cost, and letting it settle the question
    lets an implementation cost answer a semantic one. Accepted.

  Both supports for `optional` are therefore gone, and the stated view in
  OPEN-1 has flipped to `required`. One argument for optional survives and is
  kept, marked weaker: a required field materialises a closure per rule whether
  or not anything challenges it. Section 4 has NOT been rewritten to required -
  that would be making the choice - but OPEN-1 states exactly what changes
  under it, three things and no others.

  The review also named an invariant every earlier draft missed: "Blocking is
  exact to the targeted face or rule case". Rule-case blocking is in the
  specification's own invariant table.

A false claim, carried since v0.2
  The review flagged "No registry change is needed" as untagged; it could not
  check it from its packet. Checking it against the code shows it is false. The
  shipped materialised-selector/v1 contract allows a challenge selector's
  target to name a FACE and nothing else, so a rule blocker closure is not
  expressible under it today. Corrected in two verified halves: no registry
  SCHEMA change is needed, since SelectorFieldContract already carries
  allowed_record_kinds; but every registry wanting rule blocking must widen
  that set, and this one does not. It favours neither option - both need the
  same widening - so it removes a reason v0.2 gave for optional.

v0.2 is retained and marked superseded. Nothing in it was found wrong; its
central claim was found unmeasured, and its registry claim has since been found
false.

body:
Defect bindings: a conclusion reversed, and the first cross-artifact audit

Last of the approved order. Nothing implemented, nothing frozen.

The measurement, and why its first conclusion was wrong
  DischargeRecord names no atom and a discharge closure's only key is a single
  challenge ref, so I concluded that an atom-indexed discharge domain has no
  referent and that OPEN-1 was therefore narrower than the pin said.

  Independent review found that false and I verified it: ChallengeRecord
  carries problem_face_atom, and a discharge names a challenge, so
  discharge -> challenge -> problem_face_atom reaches an atom in two hops. What
  is actually missing is that every selector key is a DIRECT field of the
  selected record and none is a path, so no selector can express a join.

  The difference decides what kind of question this is. "No referent exists"
  would narrow the owner's choice; "the referent exists and the selector cannot
  follow it" is evidence the model is missing a capability, which argues for
  changing it rather than accepting the approximation. OPEN-1 is not narrowed -
  it gains a third option it did not have. OPEN-2 is restored to the live
  question it was: compiling a rule written over w into one indexed by c
  replaces one face-level obligation with several challenge-level ones whenever
  two defects name one face, which is what battery instance B1 exists to show.

  Twice this session I read "not expressible" as narrowing a choice when it was
  evidence of a missing capability. Recorded as a reasoning error rather than
  fixed twice in silence.

OPEN-6 answered from what already existed
  Case 12 cannot discriminate the closure binding. The battery's pair C can and
  always could: P3 and N3 are both undischarged and differ only in the closure
  result, taking the obligation from LIVE to SUSPENDED. OPEN-6 is a warning
  about case 12, not a gap in the evidence.

The first cross-artifact consistency audit, and what it cost to get one
  Every previous review saw one document at a time, so none could see whether
  the documents agree. Four whole documents returned an EMPTY reply at
  finish=length, twice, even after the budget auto-raised to 32k. The packet
  became the extracted claims that should agree - 18 excerpts, 2.6k tokens -
  and it then answered. A fuller audit is not a better one past the point where
  the reviewer can hold it.

  It found two hand-propagation misses on its first run, which is what the
  instrument is for:

  - CORE_SPEC_AUDIT_V0.1.md still said "no registry change is needed" for
    rule-target blocking, a claim corrected in the pin earlier the same day and
    left standing here. Fixed.
  - MILESTONE_8_FINDINGS_V0.1.md still said the registry "reaches compilation
    at two points". True as written - two reads - and a reader will take it for
    two status-changing fields, which is false. Sharpened in place.

The ledger caught two things about itself
  A superseded transcript: two calls wrote one path, so the file can only agree
  with the later. The guard now checks the latest call per path, and a second
  test asserts every superseded call keeps its row and digests so the loss is
  visible rather than silent.

  And: the defect-bindings job ran twice with a byte-identical packet, same
  prompt_sha256, at temperature 0 and seed 17, returning different replies. So
  "temperature=0 seed=17" is provenance, not reproducibility. The script always
  said an external call is not deterministic; this is the evidence for that
  sentence rather than the assertion of it. What the ledger guarantees is
  unchanged: the exact bytes each model was shown can be rechecked.

subject: Fix two settled obligations the implementation did not meet
body:
Fix two settled obligations the implementation did not meet

"Whatever is approved from spec" read as: obligations the specification settles
outright and the code does not meet. Every [N] normative choice stays on the
owner's desk untouched - those are by definition choices the specification does
not make, and deciding one would be the failure this project guards against.

A systematic sweep of five specification regions found two, both confirmed by
an adversarial pass, both verified by me before touching anything, and both
with a regression test demonstrated to fail without its fix.

SO-1: a package's canonical identity depended on the interpreter's hash seed
  "Set-valued reference arrays SHALL be sorted by exact reference." A
  ClosedNegativeLiteral carries TWO exact references - an atom and its
  mandatory closure gate - and canonical._sort_key keyed on the atom alone.
  Two literals sharing an atom tied; sorted is stable; the tie fell through to
  frozenset iteration order, which varies per process.

  The repository's own guarded_negative_package() has exactly that shape and
  produced two different package_hash values across four hash seeds. That is
  conformance case 16 failing against a package and ITSELF, and case 16 was
  marked covered.

  The suite could not see it. test_the_same_package_canonicalises_identically
  compares two calls inside one process, and the one cross-process harness in
  the repo pins PYTHONHASHSEED=0, which hides seed dependence by construction.
  NegativeLiteralOrderTests spawns children with different seeds instead -
  testing it any other way would rebuild the blind spot that let it through.

SO-2: the provenance graph could contain a real directed cycle
  "The authoritative provenance carrier is a shared directed acyclic
  explanation graph", and "Cycles in the semantic program SHALL be represented
  by references to an SCC summary node". _collapse_cycles built its dependency
  relation from requires and derives only, so a cycle through default negation
  - a <- not b, b <- not a - was invisible to Tarjan. The emitted graph carried
  the cycle with no summary node, against the specification and against
  ProvenanceGraph's own docstring.

  The evaluator was never wrong: an even negative loop is SUSPENDED and always
  was. Only the report was. Only the blocks arc is added; whether discharges,
  protects_open or contrary_to should ever count is NOT settled, and
  contrary_to is symmetric by construction, so collapsing on it would summarise
  every contrary pair as a derivation loop.

What the sweep did NOT find is worth as much: every other obligation checked
came back met, including the invariant table row by row against its named
enforcement point and the whole ground-semantics section. Two candidates were
reclassified NOT-SETTLED by the adversarial pass and are not acted on.

The consistency audit becomes a standing instrument
  It found two hand-propagation misses on its first run, so scripts/
  consistency_packet.py now builds and verifies its packet deterministically,
  with --write/--verify matching battery_digest.py's idiom. --verify fails when
  a document changes a claim another document also states, which is the signal
  to re-run the audit.

  Its own limits are built in: a pattern matching nothing FAILS rather than
  silently reducing coverage, and a size cap keeps the packet inside what the
  reviewer can finish - four whole documents returned an EMPTY reply at
  finish=length twice, at 9851 prompt tokens, while the extract answered.

  This round it found no contradictions - the earlier two propagated correctly
  - and one stale heading, now fixed. It also warned that the same correction
  now appears in three documents and copies agree whether or not the claim is
  true. Right in general; each of the three now points at the measurement
  rather than at the others.

The decision map, and the nine edges an attack removed from its first draft

The map answers "how much is actually on the desk". Its first draft answered
wrong by more than a factor of two, in the direction my errors run.

The draft: 23 open item ids reduce to 6 root decisions.
Corrected:  23 item ids, 13 decisions, 5 items of freeze-time work, 4 notes.

The structural error, which caused most of the rest
  The draft drew most items as riding on a root DECISION'S ANSWER. They ride on
  the pin being ADMITTED AT ALL - a weaker edge, and one that puts a bigger
  decision above the root instead of below it.

  RT-2 is the worst case. The draft filed "amend profile section 6's only-path
  sentence" as a rider on RT-1. The pin calls it "the largest thing here for the
  owner to decide". The second path exists under both answers to RT-1, so
  neither makes the sentence true again; and if the owner refuses the
  amendment, RT-1 is never asked. The draft took the item its own source calls
  the largest and booked it as a consequence of a smaller one.

  The map now has three tiers - admission, shape, freeze-time work - which is
  the shape the sources describe.

The fabricated edge
  The draft claimed DF-1 and DF-2 "share one cause". DF-1's obstacle is a
  missing JOIN; DF-2's is a CARDINALITY ceiling on a key. Different facts,
  different tests, different amendments. And the defect pin's OPEN-2 revision
  exists precisely to refuse that fusion - "it is the live question, not a
  narrowed one" - which I wrote one day earlier and then re-imported the
  narrowing it reversed.

Other accepted findings
  - DF-1's scope dropped two of three acceptances the pin requires, including
    the [C] claim an independent audit had flagged as OVERSTATED.
  - REG-2 is not eliminated by id-only: under id-suffix-enforced nothing is
    added either, and the mismatch already exists in the shipped build.
  - AU-1 is an ask, not a note - the audit says "the owner may still wish to
    align the spelling", and AU-6 of the same species was called a decision.
  - SO-2 was presented as closed; its own audit paragraph says whether
    discharges, protects_open or contrary_to count is not settled.
  - DF-2 does not close case 12. Case 12 is fully discharged, where the two
    indexings agree; DF-1 alone closes it.
  - The items-cleared column counted two rows on different rules, and the
    asymmetry flattered the step the draft put first.
  - Cases 5 and 15 were called deferred research; the audit says the opposite.
  - REG-1 was demoted on a criterion no source uses, after quoting the source
    that ranks it first.
  - AU-4's reach into DF-1 was inflated - defect OPEN-7 gives two independent
    reasons, and only one is AU-4. This error runs OPPOSITE to my documented
    bias, which is worth recording: "he always errs toward closure" would
    itself be too tidy.

One thing upheld: RT-6 really is independent of RT-1, and for the right reason
- RT-1 changes which rules the question is asked about, not what it asks.

A correction with nothing to do with edges: the draft argued DF-1 is cheapest to
decide because pair C discriminates its options. Pair C refutes the UNGATED
reading; it does not separate DF-1's three, because "bind to w" is
inexpressible and "declare out of scope" is behaviourally identical to "bind to
c". No fixture separates them.

The map is derived, so it carries a staleness guard: an item in a pin and not
classified fails, and so does an item named that no pin carries. The guard found
two errors on its first run - AU-5 missing entirely, and a headline count of 24
where the sources carry 23. It cannot check that the classification is RIGHT,
and says so; that is what the attack was for.

The attack used Opus 5 subagents, not the non-Claude reviewers used elsewhere.
Same model family as the author, so a weaker independence instrument, and the
transcript says so at the top. Every finding was re-checked against the sources
by hand before acceptance.

body:
Prove the transport's no-retry and no-credential rules by planting violations

The boundary dispositions named three unaudited gaps and registered three
review jobs against them. Two of the questions those jobs ask turned out to
be settleable by running the suite rather than by asking a model, so they
were settled that way.

"Exactly once, no retry": the adapter contains one transport call and no
loop, which is construction rather than a guard. Planting a three-attempt
retry loop fires eight conformance fixtures across both the adapter and the
HTTP transport -- and the ones that fire are the failure-path fixtures,
statuses 201, 429 and 500, which is the correct shape. A guard watching only
the happy path would have passed the planted violation.

"Discovers no credential": ollama_http.py names no environment or file API,
and the absence is actively guarded -- the tests patch os.getenv and
os.environ.get to raise, and separately record every environment read
attempted during a transport call.

Both answers are stronger than a review could have given. A reviewer reading
the module finds the same absence and can only report it as an absence; what
matters is whether anything notices when the absence ends.

The third job, cross-artifact-v2, is not replaceable this way: whether eight
documents agree with each other is the one question no checker here can put.

follows, and it states plainly what acceptance does NOT do: it confers no
status on any package, and it does not amend the core specification, which is
byte-pinned. Two decisions (AU-4, AU-7) conclude a specification sentence
should change; those are recorded as errata to raise upstream, not as edits.

This commit implements the registry cluster, which is self-contained.

REG-1 id-suffix-enforced: a registry's id must carry its own version. The
suffix after the final slash is dot-separated non-negative integers whose last
component is registry.version, so an id ending /0.1 at version 1 agrees and no
shipped identifier moves. That zero-migration outcome is a CONSEQUENCE of the
convention, not the reason for it -- the alternative reading would force every
id and every package hash to move, which is the cost this reading exists to
avoid. The acceptance record flags it as the one line to reverse.

REG-3: admission checks the version a package's registry id declares. Under
REG-1 this holds by construction, which is why it is checked anyway: "holds by
construction" and "is guarded" are different claims, and the new test plants a
registry built past the constructor to tell them apart.

REG-2: refused where a registry is defined and where a package is admitted;
annotation is left for certificates already written, which cannot be retracted.

Three existing measurements are INVERTED rather than deleted. They recorded
that the version was inert, that nothing checked the suffix, and that the
version reached no engine module. All three were true and are now false, and
the record of what acceptance changed is worth more than a clean diff.

- my first edit put a pack's registry id in an engine docstring, and the

- a registry version too large to write into an id is now unconstructible,

FR-18 says a guard is not installed until shown to FAIL on a planted

by hand, by whoever remembers, never performed again while the guard it
certified ages against code that moves. A rotted guard is indistinguishable
from a working one, because both are green.

This session proved the cost twice. A constant naming the two challenge kinds
that reach a rule's blocker lost a member and 677 tests stayed green -- RT-6
was, at that moment, held by nothing, and it surfaced only because a reviewer
happened to point at that constant. Then the first guard written to close the

scripts/mutation_probe.py turns the plant into a registry. Each entry names
the accepted DECISION it would silently reverse, is applied to the real tree,
and is judged by whether the suite notices. Survivors are reported as gaps,
grouped by decision.

coverage with extra steps and buries the reader in equivalent mutants. This
repository has an authority chain -- a byte-pinned specification, then a
record of sixteen accepted decisions, then the implementation -- and each
decision is a commitment that can be quietly reversed. So the report answers
"which decisions are actually held?", which is the number that replaces the
test count. "682 tests pass" was true while a decision was held by nothing.

Seeded with six mutations, all six caught, each one an edit proved by hand
earlier in this session. The harness is proved in BOTH directions: a control

DATA does not see ADDED BEHAVIOUR.

  report-exposes-acceptance  added a `@property accepted` returning
    `self.status is Status.LIVE`. The guard that existed inspected
    `DiscernmentReport.__dataclass_fields__`, and a property is not a field.
  ground-holds-predicate     added `Evaluation.holds(atom)`. Nothing in the
    suite constrained that public surface at all.
  contrary-to-collapses-cycles  added an `elif` branch beside
    `_CYCLE_SETTLING_EDGE_KINDS`, leaving the frozenset untouched -- routing
    around the guard written earlier the same day, whose own comment claims
    "a silent addition here fails there". That claim was false.

Two new guards, each proved on the mutation that beat its predecessor. The
first checks the PUBLIC SURFACE -- every public name any engine module defines,
properties and methods included -- rather than one declaration mechanism. The
second runs `_collapse_cycles` and asserts a mutual contrary pair is not
collapsed, with a positive control showing the same shape under BLOCKS is: a
branch cannot route around a test that runs the function.

THE VOCABULARY IS SCOPED, AND THE SCOPING IS THE RULE. A first draft swept up
registry.py's six `accepts(...)` methods -- a grade policy accepting a grade, a
value type accepting a value. Those are admission questions about a contract,
in a module that cannot reach a `Status` at all. The sentence forbids inferring
acceptance FROM THE FIXED-POINT STATUS, so the strict vocabulary applies
exactly where that inference is possible. Without the scoping the forbidden
list becomes a style guide, which the file's own last test now watches for.

AND THE PROBE WAS LYING, which matters more than any of the above. It applies a
mutation by replacing `old` with `new`; the registry's applicability test then
asked whether every `old` still appears, found that one did not -- because the
probe had just replaced it -- and failed the suite. So every NON-ADDITIVE
mutation was recorded CAUGHT whether or not a real guard fired.

The noise is not the problem; the masking is. A mutation no guard catches was
still reported CAUGHT. The only three survivors that surfaced were the three
whose `new` text CONTAINS its `old` -- purely additive edits, the one shape
that could slip past its own defusal. The first run's "59 caught, 3 survived"
is therefore not a trustworthy number and is not recorded as one.

The check now stands down while a mutation is in flight: whether the committed
tree still matches the registry is not ill-answered under a deliberate
mutation, it is ill-posed.

subject: Run mutations in a throwaway copy, never in the working tree
body:
Run mutations in a throwaway copy, never in the working tree

TWICE THIS TOOL LEFT A PLANTED DEFECT IN THE REPOSITORY. The first design
mutated the real files and restored them in a `finally`; a ten-minute command
timeout killed it mid-mutation and left `binding/finalize.py` edited. Signal
handlers were added for SIGTERM, SIGINT and SIGHUP; a later run died to
SIGKILL, for which no handler runs, and left `canonical.py` edited. Both times
the damage was found by checking `git status` by hand.

The third design stops trying to win that race. Mutations are applied inside a
copy of the tree made once per run under the system temp directory, so the
restoration problem is not solved but DELETED: there is nothing to put back,
because the mutated file was never yours. A tool that can leave the repository
broken when it dies is a tool nobody runs unsupervised, and an acceptance
command nobody runs is worth nothing.

The copy is of the WORKING tree, not of HEAD --- a `git worktree` would have
been cheaper and would have silently probed the last commit instead, when an
uncommitted guard is exactly what you most want to probe.

Two things follow and both are improvements. The dirty-tree refusal is gone:
it existed only to protect files that are no longer at risk, and it blocked the
normal case of "I just wrote a guard, does it hold?". And the signal handlers
are gone with it, along with the reason they existed.

Cost measured, not assumed: ~19s per mutation against ~17s in-tree, about
twelve percent, for a 7.4M copy made once.
